title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: How Stock Is Divided

When a man owns no more than enough to support himself for a few days or weeks, he rarely thinks about drawing any income from it. He spends it as carefully as he can, and tries through his own labor to earn a replacement before it runs out entirely. In this situation his income comes from his labor alone. This is the condition of most of the working poor in every country.

But once a man owns enough to support himself for months or years, he naturally tries to draw an income from most of it, holding back only as much for immediate use as will keep him going until that income starts coming in. His whole stock therefore splits into two parts. The part he expects to yield this income is called his capital. The other part is what covers his immediate consumption, and it takes one of three forms: first, the share of his total stock that was set aside for this purpose from the start; second, his income, from whatever source, as it gradually arrives; or third, things bought with either of these in earlier years that are not yet fully used up, such as a supply of clothes, household furniture, and the like. The stock people normally keep back for their own immediate use consists of one, another, or all three of these.
There are two distinct ways a capital can be used to yield its owner an income or profit.

First, it can be used to grow, manufacture, or buy goods and then sell them again at a profit. Capital used this way yields its owner no income or profit as long as it stays in his hands or keeps the same form. A merchant's goods bring him no income or profit until he sells them for money, and that money brings just as little until it is exchanged again for goods. His capital is constantly leaving him in one form and coming back to him in another, and only through this circulation, this series of changes, can it earn him any profit. Capital of this kind is therefore very fittingly called circulating capital.

Second, it can be used to improve land, to buy useful machines and tools of a trade, or for similar things that yield an income or profit without changing hands or circulating any further. Capital of this kind is therefore very fittingly called fixed capital.
Different occupations need very different proportions between the fixed and circulating capital they use.
A merchant's capital, for instance, is entirely circulating. He needs no machines or tools of a trade, unless you count his shop or warehouse as such.

Every master craftsman or manufacturer must tie up some of his capital in the tools of his trade. In some trades this part is very small, in others very large. A master tailor needs no tools beyond a packet of needles. A master shoemaker's tools cost a little more, though only a little. A weaver's cost a good deal more than a shoemaker's. Even so, by far the greater part of every such master craftsman's capital is circulated either in his workers' wages or in the price of his materials, and is repaid with a profit through the price of the finished work.

Other lines of work call for a much larger fixed capital. In a large ironworks, for example, the furnace for melting the ore, the forge, and the slitting-mill are tools of the trade that cannot be built without enormous expense. In coal works and mines of every kind, the machinery needed both for pumping out the water and for other purposes is often even more costly.

For a farmer, the part of his capital tied up in the tools of agriculture is fixed, while the part spent on the wages and upkeep of his laboring servants is circulating. He profits from the first by keeping it in his own hands, and from the second by parting with it. The price or value of his working livestock is fixed capital, just like the tools of farming; their upkeep is circulating capital, just like that of the laboring servants. The farmer profits by keeping the working livestock and by parting with their upkeep. Both the price and the upkeep of cattle bought in and fattened, not for labor but for sale, are circulating capital. The farmer profits by parting with them. A flock of sheep or a herd of cattle that, in a breeding region, is kept neither for labor nor for sale but to profit from their wool, their milk, and their offspring is fixed capital. The profit comes from keeping them. Their upkeep is circulating capital, and the profit comes from parting with it; it returns, bringing both its own profit and the profit on the whole price of the animals, in the price of the wool, the milk, and the offspring. The full value of the seed is also properly fixed capital. Though it moves back and forth between the ground and the granary, it never changes hands, and so it does not really circulate. The farmer profits from it not by selling it but through its increase.
The overall stock of any country or society is simply the combined stock of all its inhabitants or members, and so it naturally divides into the same three parts, each with its own distinct function.

The first is the part set aside for immediate consumption, and its defining feature is that it yields no income or profit. It consists of the supply of food, clothes, household furniture, and so on that the people who use them have bought but not yet fully consumed. The entire supply of mere dwelling-houses in the country at any one time also belongs to this first part. Stock laid out in a house, if the house is to be the owner's home, stops from that moment serving as capital or yielding its owner any income. A dwelling-house, as such, contributes nothing to its occupant's income; though it is no doubt extremely useful to him, it is useful in the way his clothes and household furniture are, which count as part of his spending, not his income. If it is rented out to a tenant, then since the house itself produces nothing, the tenant must always pay the rent out of some other income, drawn from labor, stock, or land. So although a house may yield an income to its owner, and in that way serve as capital to him, it can yield none to the public and serve as no capital to it, and the income of the whole population can never be increased by it in the slightest. Clothes and household furniture, in the same way, sometimes yield an income and so serve as capital for particular people. In countries where masquerades are common, renting out masquerade costumes for a night is a trade. Upholsterers often rent out furniture by the month or year. Undertakers rent out funeral furnishings by the day and by the week. Many people rent out furnished houses and charge rent not only for the use of the house but also for the furniture. Yet the income drawn from such things must always come ultimately from some other source of income. Of all the parts of stock, whether an individual's or a society's, that are set aside for immediate consumption, what is laid out in houses is consumed most slowly. A supply of clothes may last several years; a supply of furniture half a century or a century; but a supply of houses, well built and properly maintained, may last many centuries. Even though the point of their complete consumption is more distant, they are still just as truly a stock set aside for immediate consumption as clothes or household furniture.

The second of the three parts into which a society's overall stock divides is the fixed capital, whose defining feature is that it yields an income or profit without circulating or changing hands. It consists mainly of the following four items.
First, all the useful machines and tools of a trade that make labor easier and quicker.

Second, all those profitable buildings that are a means of earning income, not only for the owner who rents them out but for the person who occupies them and pays that rent, such as shops, warehouses, workshops, farmhouses with all their necessary outbuildings, stables, granaries, and so on. These are quite different from mere dwelling-houses. They are a kind of tool of the trade, and can be regarded in the same light.

Third, the improvements to land, meaning whatever has been profitably spent on clearing, draining, enclosing, manuring, and putting it into the best condition for tillage and cultivation. An improved farm can quite rightly be seen in the same light as those useful machines that make labor easier and quicker, and that let an equal circulating capital yield its user a much greater income. An improved farm is just as advantageous as any of those machines and more durable, often needing no upkeep beyond the most profitable use of the farmer's capital in cultivating it.

Fourth, the acquired and useful abilities of all the inhabitants and members of the society. Acquiring such skills, through the cost of maintaining the learner during his education, study, or apprenticeship, always involves a real expense, which is a capital fixed and realized, so to speak, in his person. Just as these skills are part of his own fortune, so they are part of the fortune of the society he belongs to. A worker's improved skill can be seen in the same light as a machine or tool of a trade that makes labor easier and quicker, and that, though it costs a certain expense, repays that expense with a profit.

The third and last of the three parts into which a society's overall stock naturally divides is the circulating capital, whose defining feature is that it yields an income only by circulating or changing hands. It too is made up of four parts.
First, the money by which the other three are circulated and distributed to the people who use them.
Second, the supply of provisions held by the butcher, the grazier, the farmer, the corn merchant, the brewer, and so on, from the sale of which they expect to make a profit.

Third, the materials, whether completely raw or more or less processed, for clothes, furniture, and building that have not yet been made up into any of those three forms, but remain in the hands of the growers, the manufacturers, the mercers and drapers, the timber merchants, the carpenters and joiners, the brickmakers, and so on.

Fourth and last, the work that is made up and finished but still in the hands of the merchant and manufacturer, not yet sold or distributed to the people who will use it, such as the finished goods we often find ready-made in the shops of the smith, the cabinetmaker, the goldsmith, the jeweler, the china merchant, and so on. The circulating capital, then, consists of the provisions, materials, and finished work of every kind that are in the hands of their respective dealers, together with the money needed to circulate and distribute them to those who will finally use or consume them.

Of these four parts, three—provisions, materials, and finished work—are regularly withdrawn from the circulating capital, whether annually or over a longer or shorter period, and moved either into the fixed capital or into the stock set aside for immediate consumption.

Every fixed capital is both originally drawn from a circulating capital and needs to be continually supported by one. All useful machines and tools of a trade are originally drawn from a circulating capital, which supplies the materials they are made of and the upkeep of the workers who make them. They also need capital of the same kind to keep them constantly in repair.

No fixed capital can yield any income except by means of a circulating capital. The most useful machines and tools of a trade will produce nothing without the circulating capital that supplies the materials they work on and the upkeep of the workers who operate them. Land, however improved, will yield no income without a circulating capital to maintain the laborers who cultivate it and gather its produce.

Maintaining and increasing the stock that can be set aside for immediate consumption is the sole aim and purpose of both the fixed and the circulating capital. It is this stock that feeds, clothes, and houses the people. Their wealth or poverty depends on whether those two capitals can supply that stock for immediate consumption abundantly or sparingly.

Because so large a part of the circulating capital is continually withdrawn from it to be placed in the other two branches of a society's overall stock, it must in turn need continual supplies, without which it would soon cease to exist. These supplies come mainly from three sources: the produce of land, of mines, and of fisheries. These provide a steady stream of provisions and materials, part of which is afterward worked up into finished goods, and by which the provisions, materials, and finished work continually withdrawn from the circulating capital are replaced. From mines, too, comes what is needed to maintain and increase the part of it that consists of money. For although, in the ordinary course of business, this part is not, like the other three, necessarily withdrawn from the circulating capital to be placed in the other two branches of a society's overall stock, it must, like everything else, be wasted and worn out in the end, and sometimes lost or sent abroad as well, and so it too needs continual, though no doubt much smaller, supplies.

Land, mines, and fisheries all require both a fixed and a circulating capital to work them, and their produce replaces, with a profit, not only those capitals but all the others in the society. So the farmer annually replaces for the manufacturer the provisions he had consumed and the materials he had worked up the year before, and the manufacturer replaces for the farmer the finished work he had used up and worn out in the same time. This is the real exchange made each year between these two groups of people, though the raw produce of the one and the manufactured produce of the other are seldom bartered directly for one another, because the farmer seldom sells his corn and cattle, his flax and wool, to the very same person from whom he chooses to buy the clothes, furniture, and tools of a trade that he needs. He therefore sells his raw produce for money, with which he can buy, wherever it is available, the manufactured goods he needs. Land even replaces, at least in part, the capital with which fisheries and mines are worked. It is the produce of land that draws the fish from the waters, and the produce of the earth's surface that extracts the minerals from its depths.

When the natural fertility of land, mines, and fisheries is equal, their produce is proportional to the size of the capitals used on them and how well those capitals are applied. When the capitals are equal and equally well applied, the produce is proportional to their natural fertility.

In every country with a tolerable degree of security, every man of ordinary sense will try to use whatever stock he can command to secure either present enjoyment or future profit. If it is used to secure present enjoyment, it is a stock set aside for immediate consumption. If it is used to secure future profit, it must earn that profit either by staying with him or by leaving him. In the first case it is fixed capital, in the second circulating capital. Where there is a tolerable degree of security, a man would have to be completely insane not to use all the stock he commands, whether his own or borrowed from others, in one or another of these three ways.

In those unfortunate countries, however, where men are constantly afraid of violence from those above them, they often bury or hide a large part of their stock so as to have it always ready to carry off to some safe place if they are threatened with any of the disasters they consider themselves perpetually exposed to. This is said to be a common practice in Turkey, in Hindustan, and, I believe, in most other governments of Asia. It seems to have been a common practice among our own ancestors during the violence of feudal government. Treasure-trove, in those days, was reckoned no trifling part of the income of Europe's greatest sovereigns. It consisted of treasure found hidden in the ground, to which no particular person could prove any claim. In those days this was regarded as so important that it was always treated as belonging to the sovereign, and neither to the finder nor to the owner of the land, unless the right to it had been granted to the landowner by an explicit clause in his charter. It was placed on the same footing as gold and silver mines, which, without a special clause in the charter, were never assumed to be included in a general grant of land, though mines of lead, copper, tin, and coal were, as things of lesser importance.
